app.carbonExplainer.title: Environmental Impact

app.carbonExplainer.realLifeTitle: What This Means in Real Life
app.carbonExplainer.lowEmissionsDesc: Based on documented farming practices, this production has very low direct operational emissions from fuel, fertilizer, and equipment use.
app.carbonExplainer.lowEmissionsNote: Note: This covers direct farm operations only, not full supply chain emissions.
app.carbonExplainer.directEmissionsTitle: What We Measure: Direct Farm Emissions
app.carbonExplainer.directEmissionsDesc: Trazo tracks direct operational emissions that farmers control — not full supply chain or lifecycle emissions.
app.carbonExplainer.fertilizerDesc: Crop nutrient production and field application
app.carbonExplainer.ipccDesc: When limestone (CaCO3) or dolomite is applied to soil for pH correction, CO2 is released through chemical dissolution. We use IPCC Tier 1 emission factors: limestone releases 0.44 kg CO2/kg, dolomite releases 0.477 kg CO2/kg.
app.carbonExplainer.tillageDesc: Soil disturbance from tillage releases stored carbon. Based on peer-reviewed research: shallow tillage (less than 10cm) releases ~50 kg CO2e/ha, medium depth (10-25cm) releases ~150 kg CO2e/ha, and deep tillage (over 25cm) releases ~300 kg CO2e/ha.
app.carbonExplainer.usdaNassDesc: Water usage is calculated using USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service 2023 data: approximately 27,154 gallons of water per acre per 1-inch of irrigation depth. This helps estimate energy used for pumping and distribution.
app.carbonExplainer.epaDesc: Fuel combustion emissions use published EPA factors: diesel releases 10.21 kg CO2e per gallon, gasoline releases 8.78 kg CO2e per gallon. Grid electricity emissions are based on EPA eGRID 2023 regional averages.
app.carbonExplainer.whyTransparencyDesc: When farms document their practices openly, you can make informed choices. By supporting transparent farms, you're encouraging:
app.carbonExplainer.whyPoint1: Farmers who openly share how your food was grown
app.carbonExplainer.whyPoint4: A food system built on trust, not marketing claims
app.carbonExplainer.disclaimer: Carbon calculations reflect direct operational emissions that farmers control (fuel, fertilizer, equipment, irrigation). This does not include supply chain, transportation, packaging, or end-of-life emissions. All emission factors are sourced from publicly available EPA and USDA data. Trazo is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or certified by the EPA or USDA.

education.detail.carbonMethodology.verif: All emission factors in Trazo are sourced from official EPA and USDA publications. This ensures accuracy, credibility, and alignment with government regulatory standards.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.epaGh: EPA Greenhouse Gas Emission Factors Hub
40 CFR Part 98 - The official U.S. Environmental Protection Agency source for stationary and mobile combustion emission factors. Updated annually.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.epaEg: U.S. average electricity emission factors (767.2 lbs/MWh for 2023). Accounts for the mix of energy sources in the electrical grid.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.eiaDe: U.S. Energy Information Administration - electricity generation and emissions data validation (0.81 lbs/kWh = 0.367 kg/kWh for 2023).
education.detail.carbonMethodology.ipccD: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change - N₂O emission factors for agricultural soils (EF1 = 1% of applied N, GWP = 265).
education.detail.carbonMethodology.usdaA: Farm energy use data, crop production fuel consumption, and agricultural machinery efficiency standards.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.usdaN: USDA NRCS Irrigation Pumping Plants Guide
National Engineering Handbook Chapter 8 - Energy consumption factors for irrigation pumping systems based on depth, volume, and equipment efficiency.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.pesti: Lal (2004): Herbicides 6.3±2.7, Insecticides 5.1±3.0, Fungicides 3.9±2.2 kg CO₂e/kg AI. Audsley et al.: Higher estimates (18-27 kg for herbicides).
education.detail.carbonMethodology.diese: EPA Mobile Combustion Factor: 10.21 kg CO₂ per gallon of diesel
Source: EPA Greenhouse Gas Emission Factors Hub (40 CFR Part 98) - Mobile combustion for agricultural equipment
Confidence Level: 95% - This is the most reliable emission factor as it comes directly from federal regulatory standards.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.elect: EPA eGRID U.S. Average: 0.39 kg CO₂ per kWh (delivered electricity)
Source: EPA eGRID2023 Summary Tables (767.2 lbs/MWh) + 5.12% T&D losses
Confidence Level: 95% - Based on the national electricity grid mix; actual emissions vary by region.
Irrigation pumps (deep well 200+ ft): 3.5 kWh per 1,000 gallons pumped
Irrigation pumps (standard 50-100 ft): 0.85 kWh per 1,000 gallons pumped
Wind machines (frost protection): 35 kWh per hour
Misting systems: 12 kWh per hour per acre
education.detail.carbonMethodology.ferti: Source: EPA 40 CFR Part 98 (manufacturing) + IPCC 2006/2019 Guidelines (N₂O: EF1 = 1% of applied N × 44/28 × GWP 265)
education.detail.carbonMethodology.organ: Organic fertilizers (compost, manure) have much lower emissions: only 0.5 kg CO₂/kg due to minimal manufacturing process.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.chemi: Sources: Lal (2004) and Audsley et al. for pesticide/herbicide manufacturing LCA, International Copper Association LCA Studies, EPA Industrial Manufacturing for sulfur byproduct factors
education.detail.carbonMethodology.calcS: When you log an event, we capture fuel used, area covered, chemicals applied, and equipment hours.
We apply the appropriate EPA/USDA emission factor based on the activity type and inputs.
All values are converted to kg CO₂e (carbon dioxide equivalent) for consistent comparison.
Total production footprint = Manufacturing emissions + Application fuel emissions
education.detail.carbonMethodology.examp: Applying 100 liters of synthetic herbicide over 5 hectares:
Manufacturing: 100L × 1.0 kg/L × 4.1% AI × 5.5 kg CO₂/kg = 22.55 kg CO₂e
Application fuel: 5 ha × 0.8 L diesel/ha ÷ 3.79 × 10.21 kg/gal = 10.8 kg CO₂e
education.detail.carbonMethodology.direc: Trazo calculates Direct Operational Emissions - the emissions you directly control through farming decisions. We focus on fuel combustion, fertilizer application, and equipment operation. This approach empowers you with actionable data while maintaining scientific accuracy through published EPA and USDA emission factors.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.conti: Our emission factors are based on the latest available EPA and USDA publications at the time of each audit. Last comprehensive factor review: December 2025 (EPA eGRID2023, 40 CFR Part 98, IPCC 2019). Future updates will be applied as new government data becomes available.

consumer.education.pageDescription: Understand how transparency scores, QR pages, and farm documentation help you make informed food choices
consumer.education.topic1.title: Understanding Transparency Scores
consumer.education.topic1.description: Learn what the 0-100 transparency score means and how it helps you choose food you can trust
consumer.education.topic1.section1.body: Every product on Trazo receives a transparency score from 0 to 100. This score measures how thoroughly a farm has documented its growing practices — from planting to harvest. A higher score means more farming activities were recorded, giving you a clearer picture of how your food was grown.
consumer.education.topic1.section2.body: Scores translate to letter grades: A+ (90-100) means exceptional documentation, A (80-89) is very thorough, B (70-79) is good, C (60-69) is basic, and D (below 60) means limited documentation. Look for products scoring 70 or above for well-documented farms.
consumer.education.topic1.section3.headi: Why More Events Means More Trust
consumer.education.topic1.section3.body: Unlike traditional carbon labels that penalize farms for logging more data, Trazo rewards transparency. Every farming event a producer documents — irrigation, soil testing, pest management — increases their score. This means farms are motivated to show you everything, not hide it.
consumer.education.topic1.tip: When comparing two products, a score of 85 means that farm documented significantly more practices than one scoring 55. Choose the farm that shows you more.
consumer.education.topic2.title: How to Read a QR Page
consumer.education.topic2.description: A quick guide to everything you see when you scan a Trazo QR code on a product
consumer.education.topic2.section1.body: At the top of every QR page you will see the transparency score displayed prominently in a green circle. This is the first thing to check — it tells you at a glance how well-documented this product's journey is. You may also see trust badges like 'Blockchain-Recorded' or 'Documented' next to it.
consumer.education.topic2.section2.body: Below the score, you will find a timeline of farming events. Each card represents an activity the farmer documented: planting, irrigation, soil management, chemical applications, harvest, and more. Cards with photos provide visual evidence of the practice. Tap any event to see its full details.
consumer.education.topic2.section3.body: Trust badges appear throughout the page. 'Documented' means the farm uses EPA/USDA-sourced emission factors in their reporting. 'Blockchain-Recorded' means the production data was cryptographically recorded on the Polygon blockchain, ensuring it cannot be altered after submission. These are trust indicators, not certifications.
consumer.education.topic2.tip: Scroll down past the timeline to see the farm's story, location information, and environmental impact details in expandable sections.
consumer.education.topic3.title: Why Farm Transparency Matters
consumer.education.topic3.description: How documented farming practices build trust and why transparent farms deserve your support
consumer.education.topic3.section1.body: Only 20% of consumers believe sustainability claims on food packaging. Many labels are self-reported with no verification. Trazo changes this by creating a verifiable record of every farming activity — not just a claim on a label, but actual documented evidence you can review yourself.
consumer.education.topic3.section2.body: Traditional carbon platforms have a perverse incentive: farms that log fewer activities appear to have lower emissions, rewarding them for hiding practices. Trazo flips this. Our transparency-first approach means the more a farm documents, the higher their score. Farms are rewarded for showing you everything.
consumer.education.topic3.section3.body: Every time you scan a QR code, you are supporting a farmer who chose to be transparent about their practices. Your engagement tells producers that consumers value openness, which encourages more farms to document and share their growing journey.
consumer.education.topic3.tip: You are supporting farmers who choose openness over secrecy. Every scan and review reinforces the value of agricultural transparency.
consumer.education.topic4.title: Leaving Reviews and Building Community
consumer.education.topic4.description: How your feedback helps other consumers and motivates farms to keep improving
consumer.education.topic4.section1.body: After scanning any QR code, you can leave a quick comment at the bottom of the product page without creating an account. This anonymous feedback helps farms understand what consumers care about and what questions they have.
consumer.education.topic4.section2.body: Create a free account to leave detailed reviews with star ratings and photos. Your review appears on the QR page for future scanners, helping other consumers make informed choices. You can rate the product, share your experience, and upload photos of how you used it.
consumer.education.topic4.section3.body: Your reviews create a feedback loop: consumers share experiences, farms learn what matters to buyers, and everyone benefits from more transparency. Farms with great reviews and high transparency scores stand out to quality-conscious shoppers.
consumer.education.topic4.tip: Your review is visible to every person who scans that product's QR code. A thoughtful review can help hundreds of future consumers.

tooltip.co2e.explanation: A standard unit that combines all greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide) into a single measurement. Like converting different currencies into dollars for easy comparison.
tooltip.co2e.example: 1 ton CO₂e = driving 2,400 miles in an average car
tooltip.carbonFootprint.explanation: The total amount of greenhouse gases produced by direct farming operations — fuel, fertilizer, equipment, and irrigation. Think of it as the environmental “receipt” for growing your food.
tooltip.carbonFootprint.example: Covers farmer-controlled emissions: fuel combustion, fertilizer application, and equipment operation
tooltip.usdaFactorsUsed.explanation: Carbon calculations for this event use official emission factors published by the EPA and USDA. This ensures consistent methodology across all farms — not a verification of farming practices themselves.
tooltip.usdaFactorsUsed.example: Government-published data ensures consistent, reliable carbon calculations
tooltip.blockchainRecorded.explanation: When a production is finished, a digital fingerprint of all documented events is permanently recorded on the Polygon blockchain. This proves data has not been altered after submission — it does not verify farming practice accuracy.
tooltip.blockchainRecorded.example: Your production record is cryptographically sealed and immutable on Polygonscan
tooltip.carbonScore.explanation: A simple rating that shows how climate-friendly this product is. Higher scores mean better environmental performance and more sustainable farming practices.
tooltip.photoDocumentation.explanation: The percentage of farming events that include photo evidence. Photos provide visual proof of farming practices — consumers can see exactly how their food was grown.
tooltip.photoDocumentation.example: 86% means 19 out of 22 events have photo evidence attached
tooltip.precisionAgriculture.explanation: Farming technology that uses GPS, sensors, and data to apply exactly the right amount of inputs (water, fertilizer) in exactly the right places, reducing waste.
tooltip.precisionAgriculture.example: Like having a smart phone for farming - everything is measured and optimized
tooltip.conservationTillage.explanation: Farming methods that disturb soil as little as possible, keeping plant residue on the surface to protect soil and store carbon.
tooltip.conservationTillage.example: No-till farming can store 1.2 tons of CO₂ per hectare annually
tooltip.emissionFactors.explanation: Published research data that shows how much greenhouse gas different farming activities produce. These are the scientific “recipes” used to calculate carbon footprints accurately.
tooltip.emissionFactors.example: EPA provides exact CO₂ amounts for tractors, fertilizers, and other farm inputs
tooltip.sustainabilityImpact.explanation: How this farming practice affects the environment - including soil health, water quality, biodiversity, and climate.
tooltip.sustainabilityImpact.example: High impact = actively helping the environment, not just avoiding harm
tooltip.quickAdd.explanation: The fastest way to log farming activities in under 60 seconds. Choose from 7 event types, smart defaults pre-fill common values, and voice capture lets you document hands-free.
tooltip.quickAdd.example: Log 5-7 events weekly to achieve 85%+ transparency score
tooltip.fertilizationEvent.explanation: Document NPK applications, organic amendments, and soil nutrients. Includes concentration validation to ensure accurate carbon calculations and consumer transparency.
tooltip.fertilizationEvent.example: NPK 10-10-10 applied at 100 kg/hectare = detailed transparency record
tooltip.irrigationEvent.explanation: Record water management practices including volume, method (drip, sprinkler, flood), and duration. Shows consumers your water stewardship and resource efficiency.
tooltip.irrigationEvent.example: Drip irrigation uses 25-50% less water than flood methods
tooltip.pestControlEvent.explanation: Document pest management including IPM practices, pesticide applications, and beneficial insect releases. Consumers value transparency about crop protection methods.
tooltip.pestControlEvent.example: IPM practices can reduce pesticide use by 40%
tooltip.herbicideEvent.explanation: Record weed management activities including pre-emergent and post-emergent applications. Document organic alternatives and cover crop termination.
tooltip.herbicideEvent.example: Organic herbicides have lower environmental impact scores
tooltip.fungicideEvent.explanation: Document disease prevention and treatment including copper, sulfur, and synthetic fungicides. Shows consumers your plant health management practices.
tooltip.fungicideEvent.example: Preventive applications typically use less product than curative
tooltip.pruningEvent.explanation: Record plant maintenance including seasonal pruning, thinning, and training. Includes fuel consumption for powered equipment to track environmental impact.
tooltip.pruningEvent.example: Proper pruning improves yield quality and reduces disease
tooltip.harvestEvent.explanation: Document crop collection including yield quantity, equipment used, and transportation. Consumers see your quality selection and handling practices.
tooltip.harvestEvent.example: Recording yield data enables transparency benchmarking
tooltip.plantingEvent.explanation: Record crop planting including seed variety, planting density, and soil preparation. Shows consumers the start of your growing journey.
tooltip.plantingEvent.example: Certified seed varieties can improve transparency scores
tooltip.transparencyScore.explanation: Your 0-100% score based on documented farming events. More events logged = higher score = more consumer trust. Unlike carbon scores, transparency rewards complete documentation.
tooltip.transparencyScore.example: 85%+ transparency signals strong documentation and builds consumer trust
